title: Oasis One: three peaks, one stroke and a circle of coins
summary: They present the one-stroke rule and make the family call three chalk drawings walkable or not, then climb one peak each over slope, linear equations and inequalities, and the month 1 monster gets its ending in a real circle of twelve.
materials: the field journal, open at the sprint's Euler pages
jumbo chalk and a swept patch of driveway
twelve coins, and the whole family willing to stand in a circle
the desert wall map, for the first waypoint flag

steps.title: How the oasis runs
steps.body:
Oasis One is not a test. It is the first shade of the season: the place where you stop walking, turn round, and see how long the line of your own footprints has already got.

Today runs in three parts.

First the family table. Before the three drawings, teach them the counting puzzle you invented in week 3: your own gathering, your own total, proved with the every-pair-twice idea. Say the idea's name out loud as you explain it, not just 'I did this': counting from every person doubles every pair, and dividing by two undoes exactly that doubling. Walk them through your own proof the way you wrote it, then teach it well enough that they could invent their own counting puzzle.

Then present the one-stroke rule, the one you hunted down in week 1 by trying and sorting, and proved in week 2 with the doors-spent-in-pairs argument. Put three drawings in front of the family and they have to call each one walkable or not walkable before you say a word about which it is.

Then the summit: three peaks, one for each week of the sprint. Peak 1 is slope and the law of a line. Peak 2 is linear equations, with decimals, fractions and the letter standing in both pans. Peak 3 is inequalities and the one move that turns the sign around. Each peak ends on a summit problem built to be harder than the ones before it.

Then the month 1 monster gets its ending. Twelve people in a circle, every second one counted out. Today it either cracks or it gets retired with honours, and both of those are respectable endings. Only pretending counts as failing.

A climb is not a test. If a summit problem slows you down, that is the desert doing its job, not a mark against you. Keep the field journal open the whole way, and copy the chalk drawings into it before anyone walks across them.

steps.title: The family table: walkable or not

problems.prompt: Drawing A, in chalk on the driveway: a square with both of its diagonals drawn in. That makes five corners, the four corners of the square plus the point in the middle where the two diagonals cross. True or false: the whole drawing can be traced without lifting the pencil and without going over any line twice.
explanation: Count the lines meeting at each corner. The middle point has four, which is even.
Each corner of the square has three: two sides and one diagonal. All four are odd.
A corner you only pass through spends its lines in pairs, one in and one out. So an odd corner has to be a start or a finish.
One stroke has one start and one finish, so it pays for two odd corners. Four is two too many.
problems.useAgain: when a drawing has to be traced in one stroke and you want the answer before you waste a single attempt.
hints: Do not try to trace it yet. Count the lines meeting at every corner first, the middle one included.
Sort the corners into two piles, even and odd, and count the odd pile.
problems.socraticHint: Where in a one-stroke trace can a corner be visited an odd number of times, and how many such places does one stroke have?

variant.prompt: Drawing B is the same square with only one diagonal drawn in, corner to opposite corner. True or false: that one can be traced without lifting the pencil and without going over any line twice.

problems.prompt: Konigsberg, chalked out at full size. Two riverbanks and two islands, joined by seven bridges: the north bank touches 3 bridges, the south bank touches 3, the big island touches 5 and the small island touches 3. Now the city builds one more bridge, running straight from the north bank to the south bank. After that bridge opens, how many of the four land pieces touch an odd number of bridges?
explanation: A bridge has two ends, so a new one moves exactly two of the four counts.
It lands on the north bank and the south bank, taking each from 3 bridges to 4.
Both of those were odd and both are now even, while the islands still touch 5 and 3.
That leaves two odd land pieces, which is few enough for one walk: it starts on one and finishes on the other.
problems.useAgain: when a graph gains or loses a line and you want to know what that does to the odd corners without redrawing it.
hints: A new bridge only touches the two pieces of land it lands on. Leave the other two counts exactly as they were.
Write the four counts in a row, change the two the bridge touches, then circle the odd ones.
problems.socraticHint: One bridge, two ends. How many of the four counts could a single bridge possibly move?

variant.prompt: Suppose the city builds two new bridges instead, both of them running from the north bank straight to the south bank. After both open, how many of the four land pieces touch an odd number of bridges?

problems.prompt: Drawing C: three squares in a row, chalked like a strip of three boxes sharing their walls. That is eight corners, four along the top and four along the bottom, with the two shared walls standing between them. True or false: the strip can be traced in one stroke with no line gone over twice.
explanation: The four corners at the two ends of the strip have two lines each, one along and one down.
The four corners where a shared wall meets an edge have three lines each: two along and one down.
Three is odd, so the strip carries four odd corners, and one stroke pays for two.
The total number of lines never comes into it. Only the odd corners decide.
problems.useAgain: when a drawing is big enough that trying to trace it would take longer than counting its corners.
hints: Do not count the lines in the whole strip. Go corner by corner and ask how many lines meet there.
The corners at the two ends are not like the corners in the middle. Handle those two groups separately.
problems.socraticHint: Which corners of this strip does a shared wall touch, and what does that wall do to their counts?

variant.prompt: Now only two squares in a row, six corners in all, with one shared wall between them. True or false: that strip can be traced in one stroke with no line gone over twice.

steps.title: Present the rule, then run the table
steps.prompt:
Gather the family at the driveway with the chalk in your hand.

First, present the rule the way you found it, not the way a book would. Say that in week 1 you tried drawings and sorted them into two piles, walkable and not, and that the pile a drawing landed in had nothing to do with how many lines it had. Then say what did decide it: count the lines meeting at each corner, count how many of those counts are odd, and if more than two are odd the drawing cannot be done in one stroke.

Then give the reason, because a rule with no reason is a spell. A corner you only pass through uses one line coming in and one going out, so it spends its lines in pairs and its count comes out even. That leaves only two corners allowed to be odd: the one the pencil starts at and the one it finishes at.

Then run the table. Chalk drawing A, then drawing B, then drawing C, and after each one the family calls it walkable or not before you say anything. Let a wrong call stand for a moment, then hand them the chalk and let them try it. Being wrong and then failing to trace it teaches more than being told.

One more piece of the rule before you invite anyone to attack it, because it is the first thing they will find. The counting only decides drawings that are all in one piece. Two separate squares chalked a few steps apart have no odd corners at all, so the counting on its own would wave them through, and still nobody can trace them, because the pencil has to lift to cross the gap. So say the whole rule out loud: if the drawing is all joined up, then no odd corners or exactly two means one stroke does it, and more than two means nothing does. If it is in two pieces, it needs at least two strokes whatever the corners say.

Finish on the invitation: ask anyone in the room to draw you a shape they think will beat the rule, and tell them the two separate pieces trick is already taken.

steps.title: Summit: three peaks over the sprint

problems.prompt: Peak 1, slope. Your dawn walk log says you had covered 260 meters at minute 4 and 585 meters at minute 9, and you held the same pace the whole way. How many meters per minute were you walking?
explanation: Slope is a per, so look only at what changed between the two readings.
Distance grew by 585 less 260, which is 325 meters, and time grew by 5 minutes.
Same pace means those 325 meters were shared evenly over the 5 minutes, and 325 divided by 5 is 65.
Say it with the unit: 65 meters for every one minute.
problems.useAgain: when two readings of one steady thing are given and you want the rate hiding between them.
hints: You are not asked where you were, you are asked how fast. What changed between the two readings?
Work out the change in meters and the change in minutes, then share one out across the other.
problems.socraticHint: Why does the minute-4 reading of 260 meters not give you the pace on its own?

variant.prompt: The log says 322 meters at minute 5 and 742 meters at minute 11, same pace all the way. How many meters per minute were you walking?

problems.prompt: Peak 1, the law of a line. Suppose a lemonade table costs you 12 dollars in supplies before you sell anything, and every cup sold brings in 3 dollars, so profit after x cups follows y = 3x - 12. What is the profit after 9 cups?
explanation: Read the law one piece at a time. The 3 is what one more cup adds, and the 12 taken away is where the table starts.
Nine cups bring in 3 times 9, which is 27 dollars.
The supplies were spent whether anyone came or not, so they come off: 27 less 12 is 15.00 dollars.
problems.useAgain: when a story has one fixed amount and one repeating step, and you want any point on it without drawing the line.
hints: Before you put any number in, say out loud what the 3 does and what the 12 does.
Put 9 where the x is and work the two pieces separately before you join them.
problems.socraticHint: The law starts below zero. What does a negative profit mean on a table that has not sold anything yet?

variant.prompt: Same table on a different day: supplies cost 15 dollars and each cup brings in 4 dollars, so y = 4x - 15. What is the profit after 7 cups?

problems.prompt: Peak 1 summit. A chalk line on the driveway grid passes through the point (2, 7) and the point (5, 16). Which law belongs to that line?
explanation: Slope first. Three steps across take the line from 7 up to 16, so it climbs 3 each step.
That rules out y = 9x + 1 and y = x + 5, since neither steps by 3.
Test a point on the two that are left. At x = 2, y = 3x - 1 gives 5, not 7.
Only y = 3x + 1 fits both points, so slope alone was never enough.
problems.useAgain: when two points are given and you want the whole law of the line, not just how steep it is.
hints: Work out the climb per step across before you look at any of the four laws.
Two of the laws will survive the slope test. Feed one of the given points into each and see which one holds.
problems.socraticHint: If two different laws can share a slope, what else has to be different about the lines they draw?

variant.prompt: A chalk line passes through the point (1, 5) and the point (4, 17). Which law belongs to it?

problems.prompt: Peak 2, the letter in both pans. Solve 5n - 3 = 2n + 12. What is n?
explanation: The letter stands in both pans, so clear it out of one. Take 2n off both sides for 3n - 3 = 12.
Add 3 to both sides to lift the number off the letter: 3n = 15.
Split both pans into three equal shares, and n is 5.
Check it forwards. Five 5s less 3 is 22, and two 5s plus 12 is 22.
problems.useAgain: when the letter turns up on both sides of the equals sign and neither side is ready to be undone yet.
hints: You cannot undo a side that still holds the letter. What move would clear the letter out of one pan?
Take the smaller count of n off both sides and look at what each pan is left holding.
problems.socraticHint: Both pans hold n. Which pan would you rather the letter end up in, and what makes that one easier?

problems.prompt: Peak 2, decimals in front of the letter. Solve 0.4n + 1.2 = 3.6. What is n?
explanation: A decimal changes nothing about which moves are legal. Take 1.2 off both sides for 0.4n = 2.4.
Share both pans by 0.4 and read them as tenths: four tenths go into twenty-four tenths six times.
So n is 6, and forwards it checks: 0.4 times 6 is 2.4, plus 1.2 is 3.6.
problems.useAgain: when the numbers arrive as decimals and you are tempted to invent a new rule for them.
hints: Nothing new is happening here. Which of the two moves you already own comes first?
Once you reach 0.4n = 2.4, read both numbers as tenths and the sharing gets easy.
problems.socraticHint: Does a decimal in front of the letter change which moves are legal, or only how the arithmetic looks?

problems.prompt: Peak 2, a story translated end to end. Your water bottle holds 250 ml more than your friend's. Together the two bottles hold 1750 ml. How many ml does your friend's bottle hold?
explanation: Name the unknown and pick the smaller one. Let b be your friend's bottle, in ml.
Yours is b + 250, so together they hold b plus b + 250, which equals 1750.
Gather the pieces: 2b + 250 = 1750. Take 250 off both sides, then halve, and b is 750.
Check the story: 750 and 1000 differ by 250 and add to 1750.
problems.useAgain: when a story compares two amounts and gives their total, and one letter can carry both of them.
hints: Give the letter to the smaller bottle, then write the bigger one using that same letter.
Turn the sentence about the total into an equation before you solve anything.
problems.socraticHint: Two bottles are in this story. How many letters does it actually need?

variant.prompt: Your bottle holds 180 ml more than your friend's, and together they hold 1500 ml. How many ml does theirs hold?

problems.prompt: Peak 2 summit, fractions in both pans. Solve: two thirds of n, plus 4, equals one sixth of n, plus 9. What is n?
explanation: Same first job: clear the letter out of one pan. Take one sixth of n off both sides.
Two thirds is four sixths, so four sixths less one sixth leaves three sixths, which is one half.
So half of n, plus 4, equals 9. Take 4 off both pans and half of n is 5, so n is 10.
Check it forwards: two thirds of 10 plus 4 is 32 thirds, and one sixth of 10 plus 9 is too.
problems.useAgain: when fractions sit in front of the letter on both sides and you need a common bottom before anything can move.
hints: Fractions or not, the first job has not changed: get the letter out of one of the two pans.
Rewrite one of the two fractions so both have the same bottom, then subtract.
problems.socraticHint: Which is easier to subtract, two thirds and one sixth as they stand, or after one of them is rewritten?

variant.prompt: Solve: three quarters of n, plus 2, equals one quarter of n, plus 8. What is n?

problems.prompt: Peak 3, inequalities. Suppose somebody solves the inequality 5 - 2n is greater than or equal to 1, and writes the answer as: n is greater than or equal to 2. True or false: that answer is right.
explanation: Take 5 off both sides. That move never touches the direction, so -2n is at least -4.
Sharing both sides by -2 is the one move that turns the sign round.
So the real answer is n at most 2, not n at least 2.
Test it: n = 0 gives 5, which is bigger than 1, but the written answer shuts 0 out.
problems.useAgain: when a solved inequality is handed to you and you want to test it instead of trusting it.
hints: Solve it yourself, one legal move at a time, and only then compare the two answers.
Cheap test: find one number that fits the original and see whether the written answer lets it in.
problems.socraticHint: Which single step in this solve is the one that could have turned the direction of the sign?

variant.prompt: Suppose somebody solves the inequality 9 - 3n is greater than 3, and writes the answer as: n is less than 2. True or false: that answer is right.

problems.prompt: Peak 3, the flip, worked from legal moves and not from a chant. Which of these says exactly the same thing as: -2n is greater than 10?
explanation: Try numbers before deciding. Put n = -6 in: -2 times -6 is 12, which beats 10, so -6 belongs.
Put n = -4 in and you get 8, which does not beat 10, so -4 is out.
The answer must hold -6 and refuse -4, so it is the numbers below -5.
Sharing by a negative walked the line backwards, and the sign turned with it.
problems.useAgain: when the letter is multiplied by a negative and you have to decide which way the inequality faces.
hints: Do not divide yet. Pick a number well below zero and try it in the original.
Find one number that works and one that does not, then ask which option holds the first and refuses the second.
problems.socraticHint: Multiplying by a negative turns the whole number line round. What does a turn like that do to the words bigger and smaller?

variant.prompt: Which of these says exactly the same thing as: -3n is greater than 12?

problems.prompt: Peak 3 summit, two conditions at once. How many whole numbers n make both of these true at the same time: 2n - 5 is greater than -3, and 2n - 5 is at most 7?
explanation: Two solves, one condition at a time. Add 5 to the first: 2n is more than 2, so n is more than 1.
Add 5 to the second: 2n is at most 12, so n is at most 6.
The whole numbers above 1 and no higher than 6 are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
That is 5 of them. More than 1 shuts 1 out, and at most 6 lets 6 in.
problems.useAgain: when two conditions have to hold together and you want the stretch of the line where they overlap.
hints: Solve each condition on its own, down to a plain sentence about n.
Draw both answers on the same number line and look only at where the two shadings sit on top of each other.
problems.socraticHint: One end shuts its own number out and the other lets its number in. Which is which here, and what would swapping them do to the count?

variant.prompt: How many whole numbers n make both of these true at the same time: 2n - 6 is greater than -4, and 2n - 6 is at most 8?

problems.prompt: The month 1 monster gets its ending today, cracked or retired with honours. Twelve people stand in a circle, numbered 1 to 12. Number 1 stays in, number 2 is out, number 3 stays in, number 4 is out, and the counting keeps going round and round, always removing every second person still standing. Which number is the last one left? Run it with coins, do the small circles first, then say why the pattern is what it is.

mustMention: do the small circles first and write the survivor for each
one lap leaves the odd numbers and hands you the same puzzle at half the size
the survivor resets to 1 at every doubling number and then climbs by two
number 9 is the last one left

explanation: Do not start with twelve. Lay coins out and run circles of 1 through 7, writing the survivor each time: 1, 1, 3, 1, 3, 5, 7.
The survivor drops back to 1 at 1, at 2 and at 4, which are the doubling numbers, and climbs by 2 between them.
A pattern is not a reason yet, so go round the circle once. Every even number goes out, the odd ones stay, and because 12 is even the counting lands back on person 1.
He is still in and about to stay. One lap leaves 6 people in a circle with the first of them about to stay, which is the same puzzle, half the size.
Twelve is 8 plus 4, so start at the doubling number 8, which resets the survivor to number one. Each of the 4 people past it pushes the survivor up by 2, landing on person 9.
The eerie part, if you want it. Write 12 in binary as 1100 and move the leading 1 to the back. Two symbols were enough to hold the whole answer, and 1001 is 9.
problems.useAgain: when a circle or a list is too big to run by hand and the small cases will hand you the rule.
hints: Twelve is too many to see. Run circles of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 with coins and write down the survivor for each.
Watch what one full lap of the circle does. Who is gone, who is left, and who is about to be counted next?
problems.socraticHint: After one lap the circle is half the size. What would you need to know about that smaller circle to answer the big one without running it?

variant.prompt: Same rule, bigger circle: twenty-five people, numbered 1 to 25, every second one counted out. Which number is the last one left, and how did the doubling numbers get you there?

mustMention: 16 is the biggest doubling number at or below 25
that leaves 9 people past the doubling number
each one past it pushes the survivor up by two
number 19 is the last one left

steps.title: Explain it
steps.prompt:
Write the ending of the Josephus monster for somebody who was not standing in the circle, one idea per sentence.

Start where you started, with the small circles and the survivors you wrote down, not with the answer. Then the move that turns a pattern into a reason: one lap round the circle removes every even number and hands you the same puzzle at half the size, with a new set of names on the coins. Then the doubling numbers, and the climb of two past each one. Put 9 at the end, where your reader can arrive at it the way you did.

If the crack never came today, write that instead, and write down exactly which small circle stopped making sense to you. That sentence is worth more to the next person than a borrowed answer, and this monster retires with honours either way.
